title: Heat Measurement and Specific Heat Capacity
summary: How heat moves, units of heat, specific heat capacity, the formula Q = mcΔθ and worked examples.

p: Heat is energy that flows from a hot place to a cold place. It travels by conduction (through solids), convection (in liquids and gases) and radiation (as waves, like the heat from the Sun). The SI unit of heat is the joule (J). An older unit is the calorie: 1 calorie = 4.186 J. Heat is a scalar quantity.
Different materials need different amounts of heat to warm up. A pot of water takes much longer to heat than an equal mass of iron.
Specific heat capacity (c) is the amount of heat needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1 °C (or 1 K). Its unit is joule per kilogram per kelvin (J/kg K).
The heat Q needed (or given out) is Q = m c Δθ, where m = mass in kg, c = specific heat capacity and Δθ = change of temperature (final minus initial).

Water has a very high specific heat capacity. It takes a lot of heat to warm up and gives out a lot when it cools. That is why the sea stays cooler than the land during the day, why hot water bottles keep us warm, and why water is used to cool car engines.
The heat capacity (C) of a whole body is the heat needed to raise its temperature by 1 K. Heat capacity = mass x specific heat capacity, so C = mc. Its unit is J/K. So Q = C Δθ.
Take your time with the numbers.

b: Heat needed to raise 1.5 kg of water from 25 °C to 100 °C: Q = mcΔθ = 1.5 x 4200 x (100 - 25) = 6300 x 75 = 472 500 J.
A 2 kg metal needs 7200 J to rise from 20 °C to 80 °C. c = Q / (mΔθ) = 7200 / (2 x 60) = 60 J/kg K.
How much heat is given out when 3 kg of iron cools from 150 °C to 50 °C? Q = 3 x 460 x 100 = 138 000 J.

activity: Take two equal cups, one with water and one with dry sand. Put them in the sun for 30 minutes and then feel which is hotter. Explain the difference using specific heat capacity.

title: Latent Heat
summary: What latent heat is, latent heat of fusion and vaporisation, the formula Q = mL, and worked examples.

sections.h: Heat that does not change the temperature
p: When you heat ice, its temperature rises to 0 °C. Then it starts melting, and while it melts the temperature stays at 0 °C, even though you keep supplying heat. The same thing happens when water boils: it stays at 100 °C. The heat is not raising the temperature; it is breaking the forces that hold the particles together.
Latent heat is the heat energy absorbed or released when a substance changes state without any change of temperature.
Specific latent heat of fusion (Lf): the heat needed to change 1 kg of a solid to a liquid at its melting point, without a change of temperature.
Specific latent heat of vaporisation (Lv): the heat needed to change 1 kg of a liquid to a gas at its boiling point, without a change of temperature.
Formula: Q = mL, where m is the mass (kg) and L is the specific latent heat (J/kg).
The same amounts of heat are given out in the reverse changes (freezing and condensing).

sections.h: Why steam burns more than boiling water
p: Steam at 100 °C carries 2.26 million joules of extra heat per kilogram compared with water at 100 °C. When steam touches your skin and turns back to water, it gives out all that latent heat, so it burns much more than boiling water. Sweating cools you for the same reason: sweat takes latent heat from your skin when it evaporates.
Check the calculation each time.

b: A 0.5 kg substance absorbs 167 000 J to vaporise. L = Q / m = 167 000 / 0.5 = 334 000 J/kg.
A 0.3 kg substance melts at 0 °C using 100 000 J. Lf = 100 000 / 0.3 = 3.33 x 10⁵ J/kg.
Heat needed to melt 2 kg of ice at 0 °C: Q = mL = 2 x 3.34 x 10⁵ = 6.68 x 10⁵ J.

A box of volume 0.28 m³ is 70% filled with iron filings at 25 °C. Find the energy to melt 10% of the filings. (Density of iron 8000 kg/m³, latent heat of fusion 1.38 x 10⁵ J/kg, specific heat capacity 460 J/kg K, melting point 1500 °C.) Mass of filings = 0.28 x 0.70 x 8000 = 1568 kg. 10% of this = 156.8 kg. Heat to warm it from 25 °C to 1500 °C: mcΔθ = 156.8 x 460 x 1475 = 1.064 x 10⁸ J. Heat to melt it: mL = 156.8 x 1.38 x 10⁵ = 2.16 x 10⁷ J. Total = 1.064 x 10⁸ + 0.216 x 10⁸ = 1.28 x 10⁸ J.

activity: Put an ice cube in a cup with a thermometer. Record the temperature every minute while it melts. What do you notice about the reading while the ice is melting? Explain with latent heat.

title: Calorimetry and the Method of Mixtures
summary: How heat exchange is measured, the rule heat lost = heat gained, and worked examples with mixtures and electric heaters.

p: Calorimetry is the measurement of the heat exchanged in a physical or chemical process. The container used is called a calorimeter. It is usually a thin metal can (copper or aluminium) with a lid, surrounded by an insulator, so that very little heat is lost to the air.

When a hot substance is mixed with a cold one and no heat escapes to the surroundings, the heat lost by the hot substance equals the heat gained by the cold substance (and the calorimeter): heat lost = heat gained.
Using Q = mcΔθ on both sides gives a simple equation. The final temperature is the same for everything in the mixture.
Method of mixtures: mix hot and cold substances and measure the final temperature.
Electrical method: a heater of known power (P = VI) supplies heat for a measured time, so the energy supplied is E = VIt = Pt.
Using a temperature change: apply Q = mcΔθ to a substance whose specific heat capacity is known.
200 g of water at 80 °C is mixed with 300 g of water at 20 °C. Find the final temperature. (Ignore heat losses.)

b: Let the final temperature be θ. Heat lost by hot water = 0.2 x 4200 x (80 - θ). Heat gained by cold water = 0.3 x 4200 x (θ - 20).

p: A nursing mother prepared baby's milk at 85 °C. To cool 300 g of the milk to 40 °C, she placed the bottle in an aluminium bowl of heat capacity 90 J/K containing 500 g of water at 26 °C. Find the specific heat capacity of the milk. (Specific heat capacity of water = 4200 J/kg K; neglect heat losses and the heat capacity of the bottle.)

b: Heat lost by the milk = heat gained by the water + heat gained by the bowl.

p: A 40 V electric heater supplies a current of 12 A to a body of mass 1.5 kg that is already at its melting point. The body melts completely, then its temperature rises by 60 °C in a further 72 s. Find its specific heat capacity.

b: Energy supplied in the 72 s = VIt = 40 x 12 x 72 = 34 560 J.
This energy raised the temperature by 60 °C: 34 560 = 1.5 x c x 60 = 90c.

title: The Particulate Nature of Matter
summary: What matter is, the idea that all matter is made of particles, and how particles are arranged in solids, liquids and gases.

p: Matter is anything that has mass and takes up space (volume). A stone, water and air are all matter. Light and sound are not matter, because they have no mass.

sections.h: Matter is made of tiny particles
p: The particulate nature of matter means that all matter is made of very small separate pieces called particles. Depending on the substance, the particles are atoms, molecules or ions. An atom is the smallest particle of an element. A molecule is a group of two or more atoms joined together (water molecules are made of two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom). An ion is an atom, or group of atoms, that carries an electric charge.

The particles are extremely small and cannot be seen with the naked eye. They are always moving. They attract each other with forces called intermolecular forces. There are spaces between the particles, and these spaces are large in gases.
The picture shows the three states of matter, solid, liquid and gas, and how the particles are arranged in each. Read the table below as well.

p: When a solid is heated, its particles gain energy and vibrate harder until they break out of their fixed positions: the solid melts into a liquid. With more heat the particles move faster and escape from the liquid: the liquid boils (or evaporates) into a gas. When a gas is cooled, the particles slow down and come together again (condensation), and when a liquid is cooled, it freezes. All these changes show that matter is made of particles whose motion depends on the amount of energy they have.

title: Diffusion, Brownian Motion and the Kinetic Theory
summary: Evidence that particles move: diffusion and Brownian motion, the kinetic theory of matter, and its everyday applications.

p: Diffusion is the spreading of particles from a region where there are many of them (high concentration) to a region where there are fewer (low concentration), until they are evenly spread. It happens fastest in gases, slower in liquids and very slowly in solids.

Examples: perfume spreads through a room; a drop of ink spreads through a glass of water; crystals of potassium permanganate placed in water colour all of the water without stirring; the smell of cooking gas or fried plantain spreads from the kitchen to the house.
Explanation: the particles are always moving and bumping into each other, so over time they spread out evenly.

Brownian motion is the random, zig-zag movement of tiny visible particles, such as pollen grains in water or smoke particles in air, caused by collisions with the much smaller, invisible molecules of the fluid around them. It was first seen by Robert Brown with pollen grains.

You can see it by looking at smoke in a small glass cell with a microscope. The smoke specks dance about randomly. This is strong evidence that the molecules of air are always moving and that matter is made of particles.

The kinetic theory explains the behaviour of matter by the motion of its particles. Its main ideas are: matter is made of very small particles; the particles are always in constant random motion; there are spaces between the particles; collisions between particles and with the walls of the container are perfectly elastic (no energy is lost); temperature is a measure of the average kinetic energy of the particles; and the forces between particles are strong in solids, weaker in liquids and almost zero in gases.
Perfume spreading in air is diffusion in gases.
Sugar dissolving in water is particles mixing and spreading.
A car tyre becomes harder in the afternoon because the air molecules gain kinetic energy and hit the tyre wall harder.
A refrigerator works using latent heat and the motion of molecules.
Boiling water produces steam because the molecules move so fast that they escape from the liquid.
